html:
Shirvan is a historic region in the eastern Caucasus, between the Kura River and the Caspian Sea, in what is now the Republic of Azerbaijan. From 861 to 1538 it was ruled by its own kings, the Shirvanshahs. It is shown here in 1000 and 1100.

The Shirvanshahs began as Arab governors for the Abbasid Caliphate and grew independent as the caliphs weakened. They became thoroughly Persian in culture. Their capital was Shamakhi, later Baku, where the 15th-century Palace of the Shirvanshahs still stands. Shirvan grew rich on silk and on trade along the Caspian.

In the 12th century the Shirvanshahs were allies of the Kingdom of Georgia against the Seljuks, and their court poet Khaqani was one of the great Persian poets. They survived the Mongols and Timur as vassals. In 1538 the Safavids annexed Shirvan.
